query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Segregation-driven formation of Mg-rich intermetallics channels Ti to form a predominantly TiO₂-rich surface passivating layer that enhances corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance in Mg-containing lightweight HEAs.
generation.material_initial_state: A rapidly solidified, non-equilibrium Mg-containing high-entropy alloy with a supersaturated solid solution and incipient sub-micrometer intermetallic clusters.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to a controlled isothermal annealing treatment to trigger phase segregation without full equilibration.
generation.conditions: Annealing at 600–800 °C under an inert (argon) atmosphere with controlled Mg vapor pressure to minimize Mg evaporation, ensuring controlled nucleation of Mg-rich intermetallics.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates with concomitant Ti-enriched regions along grain boundaries and within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: Induced segregation promotes the nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallics. As Ti is rejected from these precipitates, it localizes at phase interfaces and grain boundaries, where upon subsequent exposure to oxidizing conditions, it preferentially forms a stable TiO₂ passivation layer that impedes further corrosion and oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Annealed samples will exhibit a refined multiphase microstructure with enhanced Mg-rich precipitates and discernible Ti-enriched surface regions that yield a thicker, more protective TiO₂ scale, resulting in lower corrosion current densities and reduced oxidation mass gain compared to as-cast samples.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, rapidly solidified HEA exhibiting a largely homogeneous solid solution with minimal phase segregation.
generation.boundary: The mechanism is valid only if annealing promotes controlled segregation without excessive coarsening or loss of Mg due to evaporation; the alloy density must remain below ~6 g/cm³.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of phase segregation and Ti redistribution are sensitive to processing variables, and the competition with oxidation of other species (e.g., Mg, Zn) may complicate passivation.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of samples from the same as-cast alloy: one retained in the as-cast state and one annealed under the specified conditions. Use TEM and STEM-EDS to map the phase segregation and Ti distribution. Carry out XPS or Auger spectroscopy to analyze the oxide film after controlled oxidation and perform electrochemical corrosion testing.
measurements: Microstructural analysis of Mg-rich intermetallics and Ti-enrichment via TEM/STEM-EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If annealed samples do not exhibit enhanced Ti enrichment leading to increased TiO₂ formation, or if corrosion and oxidation metrics do not improve relative to the as-cast state, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The MgTiZn (TZ) and Mg4TiZn (4TZ) alloys developed in this study demonstrated a rare combination of high hardness, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance, which are often mutually exclusive in Mg-based systems. As illustrated in the schematic cross-sections (Figure 9), the TZ alloy exhibited a microstructure containing abundant intermetallic phases (Ti2Zn and Mg21Zn25) within a Ti- and Zn-enriched matrix (confirmed by the STEM analysis) and fine oxide particles (TiOx and MgO). In contrast, 4TZ presented a more homogeneous Mg-rich matrix containing solid solution domains composed of Mg, Ti, and Zn, and larger Ti rich regions. The presence of Ti and Zn in the matrix, along with uniformly distributed fine intermetallics, promoted the formation of a protective surface film (observed via XPS), leading to passivation and high corrosion resistance. Although micropores were observed in both alloys (Figure 1), which are typically expected to increase corrosion susceptibility, the corrosion current densities of the alloys remained low, suggesting that the protective effect of passivating surface films and refined microstructures outweighed the detrimental influence of porosity. Nonetheles

Initially, a mixed surface film of MgO, ZnO, and TiO2 was formed during immersion. This film passivates portions of the surface, but breakdown occurs at weak points, especially near pores or compositional heterogeneities. Localized Mg dissolution initiates where the film fails, and Fe-rich inclusions may accelerate this process by acting as cathodic sites. Ti2Zn intermetallics act as partial barriers to corrosion front propagation, although they may also participate in galvanic coupling. In contrast, the more uniform phase distribution in 4TZ leads to slower localized degradation. This model represents one possible interpretation of corrosion behavior based on the current data. Future work using advanced surface-sensitive techniques, such as angle-resolved XPS, SIMS, or high-resolution cross-sectional TEM, could reveal the detailed structure and layering of these oxide films and validate the assumptions underlying this proposed mechanism.

candidates.changes: Incorporated reviewer feedback by explicitly integrating the role of Mg in the SRO development and its impact on the selective oxidation process. Clarified that the SRO enhancement involves not only Ti and Zn but also Mg, which moderates the local redox behavior.

candidates.hypothesis: Segregation-driven formation of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates channels Ti to form a predominantly TiO₂-rich surface passivating layer that enhances corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance in Mg-containing lightweight HEAs.
candidates.intervention: Subject the alloy to a controlled isothermal annealing treatment designed to trigger phase segregation without full equilibrium.
candidates.changes: Clarified and emphasized the importance of controlling the Mg vapor pressure and detailed the inert atmosphere conditions to minimize Mg evaporation; enhanced discussion of potential competing oxidation processes and the specific role of Ti enrichment.

candidates.hypothesis: Nano-precipitation induced by post-solidification thermal exposure creates a dual-phase microstructure that inherently acts as a diffusion barrier, thereby impeding oxygen and corrosive ion ingress during high-temperature oxidation and corrosion.
candidates.intervention: Subject the alloy to an isothermal hold designed to induce controlled nano-precipitation without triggering full phase separation.
candidates.changes: Elaborated on the selected thermal window and provided justification for the formation of nano-precipitates acting as diffusion barriers. Added discussion on potential trade-offs in mechanical properties and emphasized the unique role of nano-scale precipitates independent of large-scale segregation.

candidates.hypothesis: Residual stress relaxation via mild annealing drives microstructural reconfiguration, aligning intermetallic phases along grain boundaries to foster a uniform and continuous protective oxide scale during high-temperature oxidation and corrosion.
candidates.intervention: Apply a low-temperature annealing treatment to relieve residual stresses without initiating recrystallization or significant phase transformations.
candidates.changes: Addressed reviewer concerns by adding a more detailed mechanistic explanation linking residual stress relaxation to intermetallic phase realignment and subsequent oxide scale formation. Clarified the annealing parameters and highlighted uncertainties in quantifying the microstructural effects.

major_issues: Proposed link between stress relaxation and intermetallic alignment along boundaries is not well-established and needs additional supportive evidence.
minor_issues: Role of alloying elements such as Gd or Cu is not addressed.
Linking stress relaxation directly to oxide scale uniformity remains speculative.
fixes: Cite prior work showing how mild annealing can realign second phases along grain boundaries in Mg-based HEAs.
Better describe the chemical or diffusional mechanisms by which stress-driven alignment results in a uniform oxide scale.
evidence_needs: Experimental data from annealing studies in Mg-rich HEAs that document phase realignment via stress relaxation.
Direct measurements of oxide scale continuity using cross-sectional microscopy or GIXRD.

minor_issues: Potential omission of Gd and Cu effects, since these elements may influence precipitation behavior.
Long-term mechanical impacts of dense nano-precipitates are not addressed.
fixes: Incorporate compositional variations involving Gd or Cu to ensure broad applicability of the model.
Discuss how nano-precipitation interacts with mechanical properties at service temperatures.
evidence_needs: TEM-based phase identification and quantification of nano-precipitates in Mg-containing HEAs.
Comparative high-temperature oxidation and corrosion measurements to confirm diffusion barrier efficacy.

minor_issues: Exact kinetics of Mg segregation and Ti redistribution are not modeled, which may be complex in multi-principal alloys.
No explicit discussion of the role of elements like Gd or Cu in parallel segregation processes.
fixes: Clarify how annealing parameters (time, temperature) drive Mg-rich precipitate formation in the presence of multiple constituent elements.
Include discussion on whether TiO₂ passivation competes with other oxide phases (e.g., MgO) under actual service conditions.
evidence_needs: Experimental measurement of partial pressure of Mg during annealing to confirm minimized evaporation.
High-resolution chemical mapping to validate the Ti enrichment in the matrix or boundaries after phase segregation.

major_issues: Short-range order (SRO) effects on oxidation need stronger preliminary evidence to support the direct link to protective oxide formation.
minor_issues: Unclear if mild annealing alone is sufficient to induce measurable SRO in complex Mg-containing high-entropy alloys.
Impact of Gd or Cu on SRO formation is not addressed.
fixes: Provide theoretical or prior experimental basis demonstrating how SRO can appreciably affect oxidation in these alloys.
Investigate alternative methods (e.g., more precise thermal treatments) that are known to induce SRO in multi-principal element systems.
evidence_needs: EXAFS or PDF analyses specifically showing SRO changes in Mg-containing high-entropy alloys.
Comparative data linking degrees of SRO with changes in corrosion and oxidation behavior.

minor_issues: Substantially duplicates hypothesis C with minimal additional discussion of Gd or Cu roles.

fixes: Differentiate more clearly from hypothesis C, or consolidate to explain how Gd and Cu may modulate Ti segregation and oxide formation.

evidence_needs: Element-specific diffusion data for Mg and Ti at 600–800 °C in these HEAs to confirm the proposed segregation profile.
